results.name: Required sections present
results.criterion: The lesson has an H2 section for each of: what is RAG, why it matters, how it works, a worked example, limits, recap, a self-check quiz, and key words.

results.name: Short sentences
results.criterion: Average sentence length <= 15 words AND no sentence longer than 25 words.
evidence: (41 words) An LLM is an AI model (a computer program designed to think or act like a human) trained (taught using many examples) on a very large amount of text to predict (guess the next word) and generate (produce new text) language.

(32 words) Store in an index: Save these embeddings in a searchable list or vector index (a database [an organized collection of data stored on a computer] that stores number lists for fast searching).
(32 words) Add to prompt: The system places those retrieved (found and brought back from storage) chunks into a prompt (the message or question you type to the AI) along with your original question.
results.fix: Split every sentence longer than 25 words into two or three short sentences. One idea per sentence.

results.name: Plain-English readability
results.criterion: Flesch Reading Ease >= 60 on the lesson prose.

results.name: Right length for one sitting
results.criterion: Between 850 and 1800 words (~10-15 minutes of reading for a slow reader).

results.name: Self-check with answers
results.criterion: The quiz section has at least 3 questions and gives the answers.

results.name: Verified links to learn more
results.criterion: A 'Learn more' section links 2-4 resources, at least one a video, and EVERY link in the lesson is on the list verified live during research (no invented or broken URLs).

results.name: No false or misleading claims
results.criterion: Every technical claim agrees with the reference facts. No listed misconception is stated or implied as true. Simplifications are allowed only if they do not create a wrong belief (e.g. 'the model learns your documents' is a FAIL, because RAG does not change the model).
results.reasoning: I checked every single line and claim against the reference facts and misconceptions. All claims accurately reflect how LLMs and RAG work without introducing false or misleading ideas, and avoid all listed misconceptions. I checked all specified items against the lesson text and reference facts. All technical claims and definitions are accurate, correctly describe RAG mechanics, and contain no false or misleading representations.

results.name: All must-cover points taught
results.criterion: Every must-cover point in the reference is actually taught (explained, not just named).
results.reasoning: Every required point M1 through M9 was verified and found to be fully explained with direct quotes present in the text, meeting all conditions for L2 coverage.

results.name: Every technical term explained
results.criterion: Every technical or English-uncommon term is explained in simple words at or before its first use in the body (a glossary at the end alone does not count). Acronyms are expanded on first use.
results.reasoning: I checked every technical term listed and verified that each one has an explicit, simple explanation either directly at its first appearance in the body or immediately parenthetically defined. All required terms are correctly explained.

results.name: Concrete analogy and walk-through
results.criterion: The lesson has (a) at least one everyday analogy a young Indian learner would recognise, correctly mapped to RAG, AND (b) one concrete worked example that follows a single question through every step: preparing documents, retrieving, adding to the prompt, generating.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for an everyday analogy suitable for a young Indian learner and found the open-book college exam comparison, which maps effectively to RAG. I also tracked the worked example of the college helpdesk bot and confirmed it clearly traces preparation, retrieval, prompt augmentation, and generation steps.

results.name: Fits a non-native English beginner
results.criterion: Uses common, everyday English words; no idioms, slang, sarcasm or culturally obscure references; assumes no coding, maths beyond class 12, or prior AI knowledge; tone is encouraging and direct.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for idioms, overly complex words, assumed prior knowledge of coding or advanced math, grammatical errors, and tone. The language used is simple, clear, and defines any technical terms immediately, making it completely accessible to a beginner learner. The tone is consistently supportive and addresses the reader directly.

results.name: Builds step by step
results.criterion: Ideas are introduced before they are used; sections go from what -> why -> how -> example -> limits -> recap; each section links to the previous one; nothing is repeated without purpose.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson sections against the required flow order and verified that terms are defined before use. The sections transition smoothly from the LLM prerequisite into RAG definition, benefits, mechanism, example, and limitations. Analogies such as the open-book exam are correctly introduced right where RAG is explained.
